analysis.one_liner: Delays Medicare price negotiations for brand biologic drugs up to two years when a biosimilar is in development.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 9, 2024, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2022 law, Medicare negotiates prices for its most expensive drugs, and a brand-name biologic can already get a one-year delay if its maker shows a cheaper biosimilar copy is likely to arrive soon. This bill would stretch that delay to two years and make it automatic whenever a biosimilar's FDA application is under review, a clinical trial is underway, or the biosimilar's maker publicly expects to launch within two years. If the biosimilar never actually reaches the market during that window, the brand drug would go back on the negotiation list two years later and the manufacturer would owe Medicare rebates for the years of delay.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, brand-name biologic manufacturers whose drugs were headed for Medicare negotiation would gain the most: whenever a biosimilar for their drug was in FDA review, in clinical trials, or publicly promised, they would keep prices un-negotiated for up to two years longer, and the delay would no longer require a formal request and government finding. Biosimilar developers would also gain, since their pipeline progress alone would trigger the reprieve. The bill's supporters could argue that a genuine biosimilar launch brings price competition anyway, and that the rebate backstop penalizes brands whose biosimilars never materialize.

how_it_helps.text: For a brand biologic with a biosimilar in development, the bill replaces the current one-year, request-based delay with a two-year delay that applies automatically once the biosimilar's FDA application is accepted for review, a clinical study is underway, or its maker says it expects to market within two years — so the brand keeps un-negotiated prices up to two years longer.
The bill extends the window in which a biosimilar marketed before the start of a year removes the brand drug from the selected-drug list entirely, keeping the drug out of negotiation for that year.

As a backstop, if the biosimilar is not licensed and marketed during the delay, the brand drug re-enters negotiation two years later and the manufacturer owes Medicare rebates — 75 percent of the excess price for Part D drugs and 80 percent for Part B drugs — covering the years the negotiated price would have applied.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and the federal budget would pay, through up to two more years of un-negotiated prices on expensive biologic drugs before the negotiated lower prices take effect. Patients waiting on biosimilar competition would also wait longer for the market-shift savings the negotiation program was designed to accelerate.

drawbacks.text: The delay would be automatic and triggered by early-stage biosimilar activity: an FDA application merely accepted for review, a clinical study that is simply ongoing, or even the biosimilar maker's public statement that it expects to launch within two years — none of which requires a biosimilar actually reaching patients.

The bill stretches the brand drug's reprieve from Medicare price negotiation from one year to two, postponing by two years the lower negotiated prices for expensive biologic drugs used by Medicare beneficiaries.

Rebates only apply if the biosimilar is never licensed and marketed during the delay, so a brand that keeps a biosimilar nominally 'in development' could hold off negotiation indefinitely while paying nothing in the interim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit, even on its own terms, flows mainly to brand-name biologic makers: up to two more years of un-negotiated Medicare prices whenever a biosimilar is anywhere in the development pipeline. Supporters could argue in good faith that a runway is needed when biosimilar competition is genuinely imminent, and that the rebate backstop means Medicare recovers if the biosimilar never launches. But the automatic trigger fires on an FDA filing, an ongoing clinical study, or even a manufacturer's public statement — a low bar that does not require the biosimilar to be close to patients — and stretching the reprieve from one year to two directly postpones the negotiated price cuts that are the point of the negotiation program. Weighed honestly, the design trades real, near-term Medicare savings for pipeline flexibility that largely benefits the brand side. That the bill died without action means those costs were never imposed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 9, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the bill finished with zero.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, who never faced a change that would have delayed negotiated drug price cuts by up to two years. Brand-name biologic manufacturers gained nothing from the bill's death, but also lost nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare beneficiaries; brand drug makers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 9, 2024; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Took no committee action on the bill after its referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only the Republican sponsor's name appears on the bill; with zero cosponsors from either party and no votes ever taken, the record shows no partisan split to measure.

industries.note: The bill would let these companies keep Medicare prices un-negotiated for up to two years longer whenever a biosimilar for their drug is in FDA review, in clinical trials, or publicly promised — a low bar — with rebates due only if the biosimilar never launches. The cost of that delay falls on Medicare beneficiaries and the federal budget through two more years of higher prices.

Because a biosimilar's mere progress toward the market would trigger a two-year reprieve for the brand drug, biosimilar development programs would become more valuable to brand manufacturers — including as something a brand could pay for. Actual biosimilar launches, which is what lowers prices for patients, are what end the arrangement.

Every year a high-spending biologic avoids a negotiated maximum fair price, Medicare and its beneficiaries pay the higher list price instead. The bill defers those savings by up to two years per drug, with rebate recovery only on the back end and only if the biosimilar fails to appear.
